note: Questions for vetting a commission-only high-ticket offer before you give it your time. Each has the answer that is a red flag ('risky'), why, the plain question to put to the company IN WRITING, and where the idea comes from. 'ftc' = FTC consumer advice on job scams (consumer.ftc.gov/articles/job-scams, checked 2026-11-14). 'practice' = common practitioner guidance for commission contracts, not law: check your own situation and, for money you cannot afford to lose, a professional. Edit freely.

sources.practice: Practitioner guidance for commission-only and independent-contractor sales roles (not legal advice)

questions.q: Do they ask you to pay anything to start: training, certification, starter kit, deposit, leads or software?
questions.ask: Please confirm in writing that I do not pay anything to start or to keep working with you.
questions.why: The FTC says honest employers will never ask you to pay to get a job, and warns about fees for training, starter kits and certifications.

questions.q: Do they refuse to put the commission terms in writing before you start?
questions.ask: Please send the written agreement before I take any calls: the commission rate, what it is calculated on, when it is paid, and any clawback terms.
questions.why: If the pay is not in writing you cannot prove what you were promised. A real company has no reason to refuse.

questions.q: Did they promise or hint at what you will earn to get you to join (for example 'our closers make $20k a month', guaranteed income)?
questions.ask: Please send the typical earnings of your closers over the last 6 months, with the number of closers, and how the figure was calculated.
questions.why: The FTC lists promises of large earnings in a short time with little work as a warning sign of a job scam. Real earnings depend on lead quality and your skill.

questions.q: Do they ask you to receive money, cash a check, forward payments, or buy gift cards?
questions.why: The FTC describes fake-check and reshipping scams: you are asked to deposit a check and send money on, or to handle payments for them. The check bounces and you owe the bank. Walk away.

questions.q: Is the company impossible to verify: no named owner, no registered business, or a website or contact that does not work?
questions.ask: Please send the legal name and registration number of the company that will pay me, the name of the person I report to, and a working contact.
questions.why: The FTC advises searching the company with 'scam', 'review' or 'complaint', and lists unreachable employers as a warning sign. Check the US state business registry or UK Companies House yourself.

questions.q: Is the commission rate, or what it is calculated on (cash collected or contract value), unclear?
questions.ask: What is my commission rate, and is it paid on cash actually collected or on the contract value? What happens on payment plans?
questions.why: Commission on contract value while the client pays in instalments can leave you unpaid for months.

questions.q: Is the payout later than 30 days after the client pays, or is no payout date stated?
questions.ask: On which date is commission paid after the client's payment arrives, and by which method?
questions.why: A fixed payout date is the difference between income and a favour. Long or vague payout is how closers end up financing the company.

questions.q: Can they take your commission back (refunds, chargebacks) with no written time window or cap?
questions.ask: If a client refunds or charges back, is my commission reclaimed? Within how many days, and what is the maximum?
questions.why: An open-ended clawback means you may owe money for a sale you made months ago.

questions.q: Can you not verify real customers or results (no named customers, no reviews outside their own pages)?
questions.ask: Can you put me in touch with two current customers, and share the refund rate for the last 6 months?
questions.why: If the product does not deliver, refunds and chargebacks eat your commission and your reputation.

questions.q: Is the offer in a regulated area (credit repair, lending, trading, investing, insurance) where selling may need a licence?
questions.ask: Which licences does the company hold for this offer, and do I need one to sell it? Please confirm in writing.
questions.why: Selling regulated products without the right licence can expose you personally. Ask, and keep the answer.

questions.q: Will you be cold-calling your own leads, with no stated source or number of booked calls?
questions.ask: Where do the leads come from, and how many booked calls will I get per week?
questions.why: A commission-only closer lives on lead flow. No stated volume means you may work for nothing.

questions.q: Do they want exclusivity or a non-compete without a guaranteed base or minimum?
questions.ask: Does the agreement stop me working for others? If so, what minimum do you guarantee?
questions.why: Exclusivity with no guaranteed income is all risk for you.

questions.q: Are you called a contractor but told your hours, must follow a script you cannot change, and cannot work for others?
questions.ask: Am I engaged as an independent contractor or an employee, and under which country's law is the agreement?
questions.why: Contractor labels on employee-style control can cause problems for both sides. Know which you are.

questions.q: Do they refuse to let you speak to a current closer or the person you would report to?
questions.ask: May I speak with one current closer about pay, payout dates and lead quality?
questions.why: A current closer is the fastest way to learn the truth about payout and leads.

questions.q: Is there no clear way to be paid internationally (for example Wise, Payoneer or bank transfer), or unclear who pays the fees?
questions.ask: How will I be paid (method and currency), and who pays the transfer fees?
questions.why: Fees and delays on payment routes come out of your pay unless agreed.

questions.q: Do they pressure you to decide fast ('spots are filling', 'offer ends today')?
questions.why: The FTC advises taking time to think an offer over and talking it through with someone you trust.

questions.q: Are your calls recorded without being told how the recordings are used or who owns them?
questions.ask: Are calls recorded, who owns the recordings, and can I keep copies of mine to show my results?
questions.why: Recordings are your proof, and recording rules differ by place.

questions.q: Is the NDA or ownership clause broader than the job (for example it stops you working in the industry afterwards)?
questions.ask: Please clarify what the confidentiality and ownership clauses cover and for how long.
questions.why: Broad clauses can block your next job.

questions.q: Do they refuse to say their refund or chargeback rate?
questions.ask: What was your refund and chargeback rate over the last 6 months?
questions.why: A high refund rate shrinks your commission through clawbacks.

questions.q: Did they send a written agreement draft showing rate, base, payout date and clawback terms?
questions.why: The single best sign.

questions.q: Can you name the founder and find the company in a business registry (US state registry or UK Companies House)?
questions.why: You know who you are working for.

questions.q: Did you speak to a current closer who confirmed pay and lead flow?
questions.why: First-hand proof beats any pitch.

questions.q: Do they supply warm leads (calls booked from their own content or ads)?
questions.why: Warm leads are what make commission-only work.

questions.q: Do independent customers or reviews outside their own pages confirm the product works?
questions.why: Customers who got results mean fewer refunds.

questions.q: Will you see your own call data and results (CRM or recordings) so you can prove your numbers?
questions.why: Your record is your career.
